chapter_theme: Under the heading கருமம் முடித்தல், fifteen verses on getting a task done through others: fitting one's manner to each person, winning help by affection rather than force, choosing the capable over kin, the senior or the base, allowing the agent his share, and keeping watch after the work is handed over.

162.reading: The verse says that toward those who look upright but mean to wreck the matter, and toward those who look false yet bring the matter to completion, the capable act in whatever way suits each, as one sprinkles cold water into hot.
162.nuance: Lines 1-2 can be construed two ways: either the two kinds of person are judged by deeds rather than looks, or the doer himself puts on an upright face and a false one by turns to suit each. The proverb fits both: hot water is tempered, not thrown out. The point either way is that the manner is fitted to the person, not fixed in advance.

pazhamozhi.literal: sprinkling cold water into hot water

story.act: no story; the proverb is the everyday act of tempering hot water with cold

pazhamozhi.applied_to: conduct toward others in a task is measured to each person's real nature, as heat is tempered

163.reading: Those who cannot carry the matter through themselves, after stirring the people they had attached themselves to into enmity by evil talk, run off first for their own safety, fearing the clash: they are breakers of the shard-bowl they ate from.
163.nuance: The fault is double: they start the quarrel with words and leave the fighting to others. The proverb's bowl is a humble broken shard, which sharpens the ingratitude: they wreck even the poorest thing that fed them.

pazhamozhi.literal: they smash the potsherd dish they ate from

story.act: no story; the proverb is the ingrate who breaks the very vessel that fed him

pazhamozhi.applied_to: embroiling one's own patrons in a quarrel and deserting them is ruin of one's own support

164.reading: Even with those one is closely joined to, the verse tells the lord of the hill country, a task should be taken up so that they are pleased and without slipping from what was said, for a task pressed in haste breaks down and turns into trouble.
164.nuance: Closeness is the case where one might think haste and bluntness safe; the verse says intimates too must be brought along gently and held to the agreed word.

pazhamozhi.literal: work done in haste falls apart and becomes a misfortune

story.act: no story; the proverb states the general rule that haste ruins work

pazhamozhi.applied_to: even among intimates a task must be carried through patiently and by agreement

165.reading: The verse tells a woman with tinkling bangles and braided hair that one should not say to the point of hurting 'they have no steady character, they are not straight', but take only the benefit, for those who take the appam and eat it do not count its holes.
165.nuance: It does not deny the flaw; it says the flaw is not the eater's business once the cake is in hand. The counsel is about getting the work out of imperfect people, not about trusting them.

pazhamozhi.literal: those who eat the appam do not count its holes

story.act: no story; the proverb is the eater who enjoys a holed cake without tallying the holes

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one takes the use of a flawed helper without voicing his flaws

166.reading: To have a thing finished on the spot instead of winning it by serving the other with love until he softens is like one who will not milk when the calf has been let to the cow, and is the way of milking a cow by loosing an arrow at it.
166.nuance: Milk comes when the calf is let in; the verse makes affection the let-down that force cannot produce. The arrow image also implies that force kills the source it wants to use.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way of milking a cow by shooting an arrow

story.act: no story; the proverb is the absurd milker who wounds the cow instead of letting the calf in

pazhamozhi.applied_to: getting a task done by compulsion instead of patient affection destroys what it seeks

167.reading: The verse tells a creeper-like woman that if one employs a slothful man he strives only in such a way that the task is never finished, and that forcing work out of one who has gone slack is ploughing with a lazy old bullock.
167.nuance: பாரித்தவன் is read here as the man gone slack and heavy; it may instead mean one who made large promises, in which case the verse joins sloth to boasting. மூரி is the old or idle bullock that lies down in the furrow.

pazhamozhi.literal: ploughing with a lazy old bullock and leaving off

story.act: no story; the proverb is the farmer whose idle bullock leaves the field unploughed

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a slothful agent cannot be driven to finish a task

168.reading: If one sets a man to do, dragging it out over ten years, a task one holds as central, who will do it without drawing some small share for himself, since not even one's own cart goes without grease?
168.nuance: காணி is a tiny fraction; the verse expects the agent's cut as the cost of the work, not as theft. ஆணி (linchpin) and the greased cart make one image: the central task and the vehicle both need lubricating. பாணித்தல் may also mean the employer's own delay.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no going, even for one's own cart, without greasing it

story.act: no story; the proverb is the cart axle that must be greased to move

pazhamozhi.applied_to: an agent kept long at a task must be allowed his small share

169.reading: Even after a task has been handed over to be done, one must keep directing those who would otherwise stall, for a chisel does not go in without being struck, even when it stands on a tender shoot that wilts at a touch.
169.nuance: விட்டு, 'having let go', concedes the handing over and still demands direction after it. The tender shoot makes the point that even the easiest task does not move itself.

pazhamozhi.literal: the chisel does not go in unless it is struck

story.act: no story; the proverb is the carver's chisel that needs the mallet even on soft wood

pazhamozhi.applied_to: entrusted work still needs the employer's continued prompting

170.reading: For those who have shown the task to the base, laid it on them and then sat at ease thinking 'they will do it well for us', the verse tells a peacock-like woman with a doe's glance, it is setting a cat to guard the heads of small fish.
170.nuance: Two faults are joined: the wrong agent, and the employer's idleness after appointing him. The cat is not lazy; it is the wrong nature for the trust.

pazhamozhi.literal: setting the cat to guard the fish heads

story.act: no story; the proverb is the guard whose appetite is the very danger

pazhamozhi.applied_to: trusting the base with a task and not watching it hands the goods to the one who will take them

171.reading: The discerning do not seek out an incapable man to entrust a task to, but only those of clear knowledge; even when such a man has learnt, come to know something and been rid of faults, it is better to go without than to give it to him.
171.nuance: முற்றல் is hard: it may be the old, the 'ripe' in years, so that seniority is the false ground being refused; or simply a stiff, unfit man. The proverb's words are also hard to divide (மற்று அதன்பால் தேம்பல், 'to pine for want of it'); the reading takes it as 'better to go without'.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is better to waste away for lack of it

story.act: no story; the proverb prefers want to an unfit remedy

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a task should wait rather than go to one without practical capacity, whatever his learning

172.reading: There is no need to ask whether a man is kin or not: valuable matter should be let go into the hands of the learned man alone, for the learned man heeds his master's word, and even if he does not, salt eaten by the ox is no loss.
172.nuance: The concession is the striking part: even if the learned agent disobeys, what he consumes is like the salt fed to the working ox, an outlay that returns as work. Kinship is set aside as a test altogether.

pazhamozhi.literal: salt eaten by the bullock is no loss

story.act: no story; the proverb is the farmer's salt that keeps his working bullock strong

pazhamozhi.applied_to: what is spent on a learned agent is not wasted even if he does not always obey

173.reading: When a task is set to be done under safeguards, one should not put on it careless men who make off once they have had their fill, since there is no wealth that does not cling to those who touch it, as there is no pot that does not cling to those who cook in it.
173.nuance: The verse treats the handler's taking as a law of nature, like the cook's tasting; the choice it leaves is only of handlers who care for the work. கட்டுடைத்தாக can also mean 'with binding authority', so the safeguard may be the master's own control.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no cooking pot that does not stick to those who cook in it

story.act: no story; the proverb is the cook to whose hands the pot's contents always cling

pazhamozhi.applied_to: whoever handles wealth keeps some of it, so careless handlers must not be chosen

174.reading: If those who were set up in office prove to have no goodness, the verse tells a wide-eyed woman, there is no need to say 'we will expose them and remove them': drive them off, for no one was ever robbed by agreeing to part with a black goat that was going to die.
174.nuance: The proverb is hard: இறக்கும் மையாட்டை 'the dark goat that is about to die' and உடம்படுத்து 'having consented' are read here as letting go what is lost anyway at no cost. ஓட்டி may belong to the counsel ('drive them off') or to the address. The counsel is quiet dismissal over public exposure.

pazhamozhi.literal: no one was ever robbed in giving up a goat that was going to die anyway

story.act: no story; the proverb is the owner who loses nothing by parting with a dying goat

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a worthless appointee is best let go quietly, since keeping or shaming him gains nothing

175.reading: If one greatly raises up men with no inner purity and leaves them in some far place out of reach, that, done without thinking and discerning, is letting a tortoise go into a long pond with the words 'get wet and come back'.
175.nuance: அகந்தூய்மை here is honesty of mind in an agent, not ritual purity. The tortoise is at home in the pond; sending it there and asking it to return is asking it to act against its nature with no one watching.

pazhamozhi.literal: letting a tortoise into a long pond and saying 'get wet and come back'

story.act: no story; the proverb is the owner who frees a tortoise in its own element and expects it back

pazhamozhi.applied_to: an untrustworthy agent raised high and sent beyond oversight will not return what was entrusted

176.reading: When one stands nearby saying subtle things about a task, the man who has gone into it without knowing its hidden state perishes, for on the well-made board laid out in rows the war of the dice is easy for those who sit at its edge.
176.nuance: The verse holds two people: the bystander whose advice is cheap because he risks nothing, and the doer who enters without knowing the inside of the work. புரை may be the hidden flaw or the inner chamber; either way it is what the onlooker does not see.

pazhamozhi.literal: the battle of dice on the board is easy for those sitting at the edge

story.act: no story; the proverb is the onlooker at a dice game who finds every move easy

pazhamozhi.applied_to: advice from outside a task is easy, and the one who acts on it without inner knowledge pays

links.note: Kural 814 prefers solitude to allies like an untrained horse that throws its rider in battle; Pazhamozhi 163 describes those who stir their own side into a quarrel and flee first.
links.teaches: The couplet's ally fails at the decisive moment; Pazhamozhi adds that the same man often made the battle, so the desertion is the second half of a single betrayal that begins with words.
links.list_adds: its proverb of the broken food-bowl names the fault as ingratitude to one's own support, where the couplet only weighs such company against being alone.

links.note: Kural 672 sorts tasks into those to be done slowly and those to be done at once; Pazhamozhi 164 says work with intimates must be carried patiently, since haste ruins it.
links.teaches: The couplet leaves open how to tell the slow task from the urgent one; Pazhamozhi supplies one test, the closeness of the people involved, and the cost of getting it wrong, that the work turns into trouble.
links.list_adds: it places the slow kind of task in the circle of one's intimates and adds the condition of keeping to the spoken word, which the couplet does not name.

links.note: Kural 504 tells the employer to examine both good qualities and faults and take what predominates; Pazhamozhi 165 says not to voice an unsteady helper's faults but to take the benefit.
links.teaches: The couplet's weighing of faults happens in the employer's mind; Pazhamozhi adds that once the helper is in use, saying the faults aloud is itself a fault, so the examination must stay silent.
links.list_adds: its proverb of the holed appam turns the weighing into a rule of speech: the faults are counted in choosing and not counted again in the using.

links.note: Kural 1078 says the worthy are of use at a word and the base only when crushed like cane; Pazhamozhi 166 says to win help by affection, as forcing it is milking a cow with an arrow.
links.teaches: Read together, the two divide the means by the person: affection draws service from the ordinary helper while force kills what it wants, and the couplet marks the base as the exception who yield only under pressure.
links.list_adds: its paired images of the calf let in and the arrow loosed rank gentle means over force for ordinary dealings, which the couplet, speaking only of two extremes, does not do.

links.note: Both use the chisel that will not cut even into a tender shoot unless struck; the Naladiyar applies it to the base, Pazhamozhi 169 to any agent left to do a task.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar makes the unstruck chisel a mark of base character, but Pazhamozhi uses the same saying of the employer's duty to everyone he employs, so the image shifts blame from the worker's nature to the master's need to keep directing.
links.list_adds: the quatrain uses the chisel to sort people into kind and harsh-ruled; the Pazhamozhi makes it a rule for the master after the handing over, a stage the quatrain never reaches.

links.note: 166 says service should be won by affection, not forced; 169 says even entrusted work needs striking like a chisel.
links.teaches: The two adjacent counsels separate winning a helper from running him: affection is the way to gain his will, but once the task is his, the master's prompting is still needed, so gentleness at the start does not excuse absence later.

links.note: Naladiyar 345 says a dog fed from a golden bowl still watches for others' leftovers, so honouring the base does not change their deeds; Pazhamozhi 170 says setting the base on a task and sitting back is setting a cat to guard fish heads.
links.teaches: The quatrain states the base man's fixed appetite; Pazhamozhi turns it into a charge against the employer, whose fault is not only the choice but sitting idle afterwards, so the base nature becomes the master's loss.
links.list_adds: it moves the quatrain's observation into the employer's domain and adds the second fault of leaving the agent unwatched.

links.note: Kural 503 says even those who have studied hard books and are flawless are rarely without some blankness; Pazhamozhi 171 says even one who has learnt and is rid of faults should not get a task without clear practical knowledge.
links.teaches: The verbal echo (learned and faultless) makes the pair a step: the couplet admits learning leaves gaps, and Pazhamozhi draws the employer's conclusion that learning and faultlessness alone do not qualify a man for a task.
links.list_adds: it adds the decision the couplet leaves open, that the work should wait rather than go to the learned but incapable.

links.note: Kural 515 says work is not to be given to anyone but one who knows and can do it, merely because he is favoured; Pazhamozhi 172 says not to ask whether a man is kin but to look only at learning.
links.teaches: The couplet bars favour as a ground; Pazhamozhi names the commonest favour, kinship, and adds a concession the couplet lacks, that even a disobedient learned agent costs no more than the salt fed to a working ox.
links.list_adds: its proverb weighs the risk of the learned stranger against kin and finds the risk cheap, a cost-reckoning the couplet does not make.

links.note: 168 says even one's own cart needs grease, so an agent takes his small share; 173 says wealth always clings to those who handle it, so careless handlers must not be chosen.
links.teaches: Together the two verses accept the handler's share as unavoidable and then limit it: the master budgets for the grease but chooses men who care for the work, so the cut stays a காணி and does not become flight with the goods.

links.note: Kural 510 says doubting one who has been trusted brings endless trouble; Pazhamozhi 174 says that if an appointee proves bad he should be let go without public exposure.
links.teaches: The couplet warns against doubt of a trusted man; Pazhamozhi takes the harder case where the doubt is proven, and still counsels quiet removal, so the concern in both is the damage done by open distrust.
links.list_adds: it adds the case the couplet does not face, the appointee who has truly failed, and the manner of removing him.

links.note: Kural 520 tells the ruler to look daily into those who do his work; Pazhamozhi 175 says raising untrustworthy men and leaving them far off is setting a tortoise loose in a pond and asking it to return.
links.teaches: The couplet prescribes daily oversight; Pazhamozhi shows what its absence looks like, an agent out of sight and in his own element, and adds that the fault is compounded when the agent lacked honesty of mind from the start.
links.list_adds: its proverb joins two errors the couplet keeps apart from choosing, raising the wrong man and sending him beyond sight.

links.note: Kural 664 says speaking is easy for anyone and doing as spoken is hard; Pazhamozhi 176 says the bystander's subtle advice is easy while the doer who enters without inner knowledge perishes.
links.teaches: The couplet sets saying against doing in one person; Pazhamozhi splits them between two, the adviser at the edge of the board and the player in it, so the cost of easy speech falls on someone else.
links.list_adds: its dice-board proverb puts the speaker and the doer in different seats, which the couplet's single subject does not.

links.note: Kural 677 says the doer should learn the mind of one who knows the task from inside; Pazhamozhi 176 warns against the bystander who speaks fine words but does not know the task's hidden state.
links.teaches: The couplet tells the doer to take counsel; Pazhamozhi adds which counsel to refuse, that of the onlooker who talks subtly from outside, so the test of an adviser is inner knowledge, not subtlety.
links.list_adds: it sets the false adviser beside the true one the couplet names, a contrast the couplet does not draw.

links.note: Naladiyar 350 says small bullocks never learn to draw the cart however well fed; Pazhamozhi 167 says forcing work from a slack man is ploughing with an idle old bullock.
links.teaches: The quatrain says care cannot supply a missing capacity; Pazhamozhi adds that pressure cannot either, so between them neither feeding nor driving makes the unfit beast or man do the work.
links.list_adds: it turns the quatrain's verdict on the base into a rule for the employer about sloth and the use of force.

source_issues: 174 line 4: the core text repaired ௌ written as ெ + ள in வௌவுண்டார், and the reading differs from the site; the proverb's sense remains uncertain.
176 lines 3-4: the quotation marks open at அரங்கினுள், leaving நிரையிருந்து மாண்ட outside the proverb though it qualifies the board; the proverb's start is doubtful.
171 line 4: the proverb மற்றதென் பாற்றேம்பல் நன்று is run together and can be divided more than one way.
